A user reported that after they updated their AngelList profile, AngelList emailed their employer to confirm the entry. Other commenters said it gave them 'cold sweats' and called it a betrayal of trust.

A user posted the email AngelList sends to cofounders when they're added to a profile. It is signed with the user's full name and written in first person ('I'm building an AngelList profile...'), with the user's own email as Reply-To. They said 100% of recipients thought they had written it, and that the email was sent without any preview or consent.

When adding team members to their own org, a user got replies from people answering emails sent in their name with their address as reply-to. The emails were 'deliberately crafted to seem personal.' They'd be fine with it if AngelList showed the template first and asked 'we're about to send this, okay?'

A user called the site extremely flaky: major features were totally broken and the design felt haphazard, like a mock-up. Support was 'absolutely non-existent'; several emails went unanswered. The glitches made their profile look careless to investors.
A user who is neither HR nor a recruiter at their company can still see the recruiting/candidates tab. They avoid applying to jobs through AngelList and apply directly on company websites instead.
A user quit AngelList after a recruiter confirmed seeing that their profile was actively browsing the site. They called it 'a scammier version of LinkedIn.'

A dissenting user saw no issue: confirming claimed roles or projects with the organization owner is simple verification. Otherwise anyone could claim anything, and the same check applies to advisors, cofounders and investors in both directions.
Numerous commenters said they deleted their AngelList accounts in response to the impersonation emails. One shared the steps: profile picture > Settings > Delete account.

Every time a user tried AngelList's site they hit 'a comedy of errors.' They sent several detailed bug reports to support with no reply or fixes. The only result was spam email; no contact through AngelList offered anything beyond mass-shilled pitches.

A founder and hobby angel investor said they wouldn't use AngelList Stack. They described AngelList's UX as terrible and said it's never clear how things work. Combined with slow customer support, they'd rather use best-of-breed tools for banking, cap table management and legal.

A user compared AngelList Stack to the alternatives they already use: Stripe Atlas for incorporation (smooth), Mercury as an 'incredible' bank (they expect Stack's bank to be a step down), and Carta for equity. They asked why AngelList didn't offer this five years ago when it was hard.
A user walked through Stack's signup until the documents page, then found a disclaimer excluding gambling apps. They were disappointed because they see legal gambling as a massive, growing industry.
For one user, Stack's main appeal was that Azlo, the bank Stripe Atlas used, shut down, and they didn't want to figure out a replacement.

An angel investor said AngelList provides easy deal flow but the deals are 'offensively' priced. They don't trust the syndicates: leads seem very high volume and minimums very low. They prefer building founder relationships and writing bigger seed checks.
A lawyer-minded commenter noted that Stack uses Goodwin form documents rather than Orrick. They said this makes Stack-incorporated companies nicer to work with than others.
A user wished Stack included accounting and tax services, calling them an enormous pain for first-time founders.

A user headhunted via AngelList found the app so dysfunctional they suspected AngelList had feature-flagged them a broken version as a test. They called the recruiting tool equally confounding and said candidates get ignored through that channel at their employer.

A user said AngelList was central to their last job hunt and pretty great. Being contacted directly by serious founders and technical VPs was 'infinitely better' than dealing with recruiters who don't understand the jobs.
